class.name: NetwPromise
class.brief_description: The pending result of a one-to-one network request, resolved once with the responder's return value.
class.description: It settles exactly once: [method then] fires with the value the remote handler returned, or [method catch_error] fires with an [enum @GlobalScope.Error] code if the request times out or the target peer disconnects. Chaining before it settles is safe, and chaining after a settled promise fires the callback immediately, so there is no race between sending and subscribing. [codeblock] Netw.request(server.buy_item, item_id) \ .then(func(receipt: Dictionary) -> void: show_receipt(receipt)) \ .catch_error(func(code: Error, detail: String) -> void: show_error(error_string(code) if detail.is_empty() else detail) ) [/codeblock] The settle vocabulary is closed. [constant @GlobalScope.ERR_TIMEOUT] means the deadline passed with no reply, [constant @GlobalScope.ERR_UNAVAILABLE] means the responder went away before it could answer, and [constant @GlobalScope.ERR_UNAUTHORIZED] means the responder rejected. The [member detail] string carries the human-readable reason and is never the thing code branches on. A returned [Node] arrives resolved to the live local instance, deferred until it spawns if the reply beats its spawn packet. See [NetwGroupPromise] for the one-to-many form.

method.name: answer
method.description: Returns [member result] after success or [member code] after failure. [signal ready] carries the same value. Check [member is_settled] before reading an unsettled promise.

method.name: catch_error
method.description: Chains [param cb] to run if the promise is rejected or timed out. It receives [member code] and [member detail]. A promise that already failed runs it immediately, and either way this returns the promise so calls chain.

method.name: reject
method.description: Settles the promise as failed with [param err_code] and an optional human-readable [param err_detail]. Emits [signal failed] then [signal settled] and runs every chained [method catch_error]. A promise that already settled is unchanged, because a settled promise is an answer and a second answer would be a different one. Rejecting with nothing listening warns, since a network failure nobody handles is the one a game finds out about from its players.

method.name: resolve
method.description: Settles the promise as completed with [param val]. Emits [signal completed] then [signal settled] and runs every chained [method then]. A promise that already settled is unchanged.

method.name: then
method.description: Chains [param cb] to run when the promise resolves. It receives [member result]. A promise that already completed runs it immediately, and either way this returns the promise so calls chain.

method.name: wait
method.description: Returns a [Signal] on the [signal ready] channel that is safe to [code]await[/code] whether or not the promise has already settled, carrying [method answer]. This is the idiom. Awaiting [signal settled] directly is a race the caller cannot win: a promise that settled first has already emitted it and the caller waits forever, which is why call sites grew a hand-written [member is_settled] guard. An already-settled promise defers its emission here, so the [code]await[/code] subscribes before the answer is delivered. [codeblock] var err: Error = await engine.flush(keys).wait() [/codeblock] This never re-emits [signal completed], [signal failed] or [signal settled], so an earlier subscriber is notified exactly once no matter how late anyone waits.

method.name: when_settled
method.description: Chains a zero-argument [param cb] to run the moment [member is_settled] becomes true, whichever way it went. An already-settled promise runs it immediately, and either way this returns the promise so calls chain. This is what a caller with no coroutine uses in place of [code]await promise.settled[/code]. Awaiting is a race the caller cannot win, because a promise that settled before the [code]await[/code] has already emitted [signal settled] and the caller waits forever; subscribing here has no such window. It is also the only chain that survives both outcomes, since [method then] never fires on a rejection and [method catch_error] never fires on a success. [codeblock] func answer_when_settled(operation: NetwPromise) -> void: operation.when_settled(func() -> void: reply(operation.code)) [/codeblock]

members.member: The settle code when [member is_failed] is [code]true[/code], and [constant @GlobalScope.OK] otherwise.
The human-readable reason behind [member code], empty when the code says it all. Diagnostics only, never a branch condition.
Whether the promise was rejected or timed out.
Whether the promise has settled, whichever way it went. [member is_completed] alone means "succeeded", so code that only needs to know the operation is over asks this instead of testing both flags.
The resolved value when [member is_completed] is [code]true[/code].

signal.name: completed
signal.description: Emitted when the promise resolves, carrying [member result].

signal.name: failed
signal.description: Emitted when the promise is rejected, carrying the settle [param code] and its human-readable [param detail].

signal.name: ready
signal.description: Carries [method answer]. A pending promise emits this once when it settles. [method wait] emits it later for each call made after settlement. [b]Note:[/b] connect to [signal settled] instead. Because a settled promise emits this per call, a subscriber attached by hand can see it more than once. [method wait] is its only intended producer and consumer.

signal.name: settled
signal.description: Emitted once when the promise settles, whichever way it went. Connect here when the outcome matters less than the operation being over, and read [member code] afterwards. Do not [code]await[/code] this: a signal that already fired never fires again, so a promise that settled first leaves the caller waiting forever. [method wait] exists for that and has no such window. [codeblock] var err: Error = await promise.wait() if err != OK: show_error(promise.detail) [/codeblock]
